quests.correctSentence: I have been waiting for almost an hour.
quests.contrastSentence: I has been waiting for almost an hour.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing) highlights an ongoing activity: have been waiting. The focus is on the duration of the waiting itself, still continuing now.
quests.nativeTip: This emphasizes an activity that has continued right up to now.

quests.correctSentence: She has been studying all night; she looks exhausted.
quests.contrastSentence: She have been studying all night; she looks exhausted.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'She' takes 'has been' in this tense: has been studying. Her current tiredness is a visible result of this ongoing activity.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'she' needs the third-person form of this continuous perfect tense.

quests.correctSentence: — Why are your hands so dirty? — I have been working in the garden all morning.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why are your hands so dirty? — I has been working in the garden all morning.
quests.ruleExplanation: The dirty hands are explained by an activity that's been happening for a while: have been working in the garden, matching the pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The dirty hands are the visible result of an ongoing activity.

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect Continuous vs Simple: Ongoing Process
quests.grammarRule: Present Perfect Continuous vs Simple: Ongoing Process
quests.correctSentence: I have been reading this book for two weeks; I'm almost finished.
quests.contrastSentence: I have read this book for two weeks; I'm almost finished.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Have been reading' emphasizes the ongoing process over two weeks. This differs from 'have read', which would focus on a completed result or quantity.
quests.nativeTip: The focus here is on the ongoing process, not a finished count.

quests.correctSentence: I have read three books this month already.
quests.contrastSentence: I have been reading three books this month already.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Have read' fits here because the focus is a completed count of finished books: have read three books. This contrasts with 'have been reading', which highlighted the process itself in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This focuses on a finished number of completed items, not an ongoing process.

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect Continuous vs Simple: Ongoing Process
quests.grammarRule: Present Perfect Continuous vs Simple: Ongoing Process
quests.correctSentence: — Your eyes look tired. — Yeah, I have been staring at the screen all day.
quests.contrastSentence: — Your eyes look tired. — Yeah, I have stared at the screen all day.
quests.ruleExplanation: The tired eyes result from an ongoing activity over the whole day: have been staring, matching the process-focused pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The tiredness comes from a continuous activity, not a finished count.

quests.correctSentence: By the time I arrived, the meeting had already started.
quests.contrastSentence: By the time I arrived, the meeting has already started.
quests.ruleExplanation: Past perfect (had + past participle) describes something that happened before another past event: the meeting had started before I arrived.
quests.nativeTip: This event finished before another past event (my arrival).

quests.correctSentence: She had finished her homework before dinner.
quests.contrastSentence: She have finished her homework before dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had' fits since finishing homework happened before dinner, another point in the past: had finished before dinner.
quests.nativeTip: One past action (finishing homework) happened before another past action (dinner).

quests.correctSentence: — Was Tom there when you got to the party? — No, he had already left.
quests.contrastSentence: — Was Tom there when you got to the party? — No, he has already left.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since Tom left before you arrived, another point in the past, 'had left' is correct: he had already left by then.
quests.nativeTip: Tom's leaving happened before another past moment: your arrival.

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing
quests.grammarRule: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing
quests.correctSentence: When I got home, I realized I had left my keys at the office.
quests.contrastSentence: When I got home, I realized I left my keys at the office.
quests.ruleExplanation: The keys were left behind before realizing it at home, so past perfect is needed: had left them at the office, before the later realization.
quests.nativeTip: Leaving the keys happened before another past moment: realizing it at home.

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing
quests.grammarRule: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing
quests.correctSentence: When I got home, I made dinner right away.
quests.contrastSentence: When I got home, I had made dinner right away.
quests.ruleExplanation: Simple past fits here because both actions happen in sequence, not one before the other: got home, then made dinner. Past perfect would only apply if making dinner happened before getting home.
quests.nativeTip: These two actions happen one after another, not one before the other.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you know about the change before the meeting? — No, I hadn't heard about it until someone told me there.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you know about the change before the meeting? — No, I didn't heard about it until someone told me there.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Hadn't heard' shows the lack of knowledge existed before a later past point, being told at the meeting, matching the past perfect negative pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Not knowing something happened before another past event: being told at the meeting.

quests.correctSentence: By the time the police arrived, the thief had already escaped.
quests.contrastSentence: By the time the police arrived, the thief was already escaped.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By the time' commonly introduces past perfect, showing one event was complete before another: had escaped by the time they arrived.
quests.nativeTip: 'By the time' is a classic signal phrase for this tense.

quests.correctSentence: Before she left the house, she had checked all the windows.
quests.contrastSentence: After she left the house, she had checked all the windows.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Before' introduces the later action (leaving), while the earlier action (checking windows) correctly stays in past perfect: had checked before she left.
quests.nativeTip: The checking happened earlier than the leaving, which comes second in the sentence.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you eat before the movie? — Yes, we had already eaten dinner.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you eat before the movie? — Yes, we have already eaten dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since eating happened before going to the movie, another past event, past perfect fits: had already eaten before the movie.
quests.nativeTip: Eating happened before another past event: going to the movie.

quests.correctSentence: This time tomorrow, I will be lying on a beach.
quests.contrastSentence: This time tomorrow, I will lying on a beach.
quests.ruleExplanation: Future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an action in progress at a future point: will be lying on the beach at that exact time tomorrow.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an action in progress at a specific future moment.

quests.correctSentence: At 8 pm, we will be having dinner.
quests.contrastSentence: At 8 pm, we will having dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At 8 pm' pinpoints a moment in the future, matching future continuous: will be having dinner at that time.
quests.nativeTip: The specific future time '8 pm' signals an action in progress then.

quests.correctSentence: — Can you call me at noon? — I might be busy; I will be probably still working then.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can you call me at noon? — I might be busy; I will probably still working then.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will be working' describes an action expected to be in progress at noon, matching the same pattern practiced in Questions 1 and 2.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'then' points to an action in progress at that future moment.

quests.correctSentence: I will call you as soon as I arrive.
quests.contrastSentence: I will be call you as soon as I arrive.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will' fits a simple future action or decision: will call you. There's no specific future moment where the calling is 'in progress', so future continuous isn't needed here.
quests.nativeTip: This is a simple, quick future action, not something ongoing at a specific moment.

quests.correctSentence: At this time next week, I will be relaxing on vacation.
quests.contrastSentence: At this time next week, I am relaxing on vacation.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At this time next week' pinpoints a future moment, so future continuous fits: will be relaxing at that exact time, contrasting with the simple future in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: 'At this time next week' points to a specific future moment, unlike Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: — What are your plans for the weekend? — I'm not sure yet, but I will probably visit my parents.
quests.contrastSentence: — What are your plans for the weekend? — I'm not sure yet, but I was probably visit my parents.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will' fits this general, uncertain future plan: will probably visit. No specific moment is pinned down, so future continuous isn't needed, unlike Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general, uncertain plan, not an action tied to one exact future moment.

quests.correctSentence: I have never been to New York.
quests.contrastSentence: I had never been to New York.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I' takes 'have' in present perfect for life experience: have never been. This reviews the pattern first introduced in Level 106.
quests.nativeTip: The subject is 'I', describing a life experience up to now.

quests.correctSentence: I've been studying its history for months, so I feel like I know it well.
quests.contrastSentence: I've have studying its history for months, so I feel like I know it well.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I've been studying' completes the present perfect continuous form, emphasizing the ongoing months of study, as practiced in Level 111.
quests.nativeTip: This completes the present perfect continuous form after 've.

quests.correctSentence: — Had you met her before the conference? — No, I had never met her until then.
quests.contrastSentence: — Had you met her before the conference? — No, I did never met her until then.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply matches the question's own past perfect: had never met her, describing a situation true before the conference.
quests.nativeTip: Match the same tense the question itself already used.

quests.correctSentence: By the time we got to the theater, the film had already started.
quests.contrastSentence: By the time we got to the theater, the film was already started.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By the time' signals past perfect once again: the film had started before you arrived, missing the beginning.
quests.nativeTip: This event finished before another past event, your arrival.

quests.correctSentence: We had been waiting outside for twenty minutes when they finally opened the doors.
quests.contrastSentence: We have been waiting outside for twenty minutes when they finally opened the doors.
quests.ruleExplanation: Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) shows an ongoing action leading up to another past event: had been waiting before the doors opened.
quests.nativeTip: This ongoing action was already happening before another past event, the doors opening.

quests.correctSentence: — How was the trip? — Great, though we had been traveling for over twelve hours by the time we landed.
quests.contrastSentence: — How was the trip? — Great, though we have been traveling for over twelve hours by the time we landed.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had been traveling' shows the ongoing journey leading up to landing, another past point, matching the pattern from Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: The traveling was ongoing right up until another past event: landing.

quests.correctSentence: I had been working on this project for six months, and I finally finished it yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: I have been working on this project for six months, and I finally finished it yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the project was finished yesterday, a specific past point, the ongoing work leading up to it takes past perfect continuous: had been working, then finished.
quests.nativeTip: The finishing happened yesterday, a specific past point, so the ongoing work leading up to it needs a matching past tense.

quests.correctSentence: By next month, I will have been living here for ten years.
quests.contrastSentence: By next month, I will be living here for ten years.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will have been' looks forward to a future point and counts a duration reaching up to it: will have been living here for ten years by next month. This combines the future and perfect ideas from this entire stage into one advanced form.
quests.nativeTip: This looks ahead to a future point and measures a duration that will be complete by then.

quests.correctSentence: — Tell me about your journey to get here. — Well, by the time I got this job, I had applied to over fifty companies.
quests.contrastSentence: — Tell me about your journey to get here. — Well, by the time I got this job, I did applied to over fifty companies.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By the time I got this job' signals past perfect once more: had applied to fifty companies before that point, wrapping up the full journey through perfect and continuous tenses covered across Levels 101 to 120.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Stage 6 with the same 'by the time' signal practiced throughout this block.
